doc.title: Joseph Daley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 18, 2018

title: Political message in his music and Black Lives Matter
summary: All his music carries a political statement, with the Trayvon Martin Suite and a piece for his brother.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: I was talking with Warren yesterday a bit about Max Roach.
He had a political content to his music at times. And I wonder if you guys, if you feel any of your music has a political message.

All of our music has a political message. The thing is this: as African-American, especially African-American men, there’s always a message that we can do and we can survive. Because I can just leave here and go driving down across the Thruway and then you know get pulled over by a police officer and the next morning you read that I’ve been shot. And a lot of people won’t even bat their eye, because it’s just, this type of thing just happens. So the injustices that have been put on us as African-Americans, you know, by this society and everything, every time we play we’re making some type of political statement you know. Especially like the second set — the music, I call it the revolution— this is revolutionary music and everything. And every ensemble, one of the CDs I had out last night was the “Trayvon Martin Suite” thing that I did with Bill Cole and everything. We have political — my “Seven Deadly Sins” has a huge track that I wrote for my brother called “Ballad of the Fallen African Warrior” you know dealing with his demise via the healthcare system in America. So the music has, everything that I do has a political — sometimes I don’t think it’s appropriate, like last night I didn’t think it was appropriate to address that in certain situations. But yeah, but everything that I do has to have a political statement you know, because you know, I’m a reflection of society and everything. And you know, I’ve got to let people know that my life matters too. Like the whole Black Lives Matter movement. My life matters. But the thing is, what most

people are failing to understand is because I say that Black Lives Matter, it doesn’t mean that other people’s lives do not matter, but they’re already protected in the system. You know, they’re not going to be shot down like Trayvon Martin for no reason or anything. They have these protections built in already. So people know their lives matter and they treat them with that type of respect. But for some strange reason, people, especially law enforcement and other people, think that our lives do not matter. So we’re not — Black Lives Matter is an inclusive movement. We’re including, you know we include everybody in the concept of Black Lives Matter. Because we already know that people know that these other lives matter so we just want that same type of respect. So it’s just a matter of getting the same type of respect as the other people whose lives, based on the way society is set up, their lives already matter. So we just want that same type of respect.
